name: Bill Hagerty
bio: Former U.S. Ambassador to Japan and Tennessee Commissioner of Economic and Community Development. Trump-endorsed; $5.3M cash on hand.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Hagerty has no specific 2026 statements on pre-K or Head Start. His February 2026 Senate floor remarks praised Tennessee's school choice expansion but made no mention of early childhood programs. The OBBB he supported (July 2025) quadrupled the employer childcare tax credit but did not expand direct pre-K or Head Start funding.
early_childhood_ed.details: On February 5, 2026, Hagerty praised Governor Lee's State of the State address from the Senate floor, emphasizing parental school choice and noting Tennessee has risen to a top-5 state for reading and math gains — but framed entirely around K-12 school choice, with no mention of pre-K or Head Start. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act he voted for in July 2025 quadrupled the employer childcare credit, which advocacy groups note primarily benefits higher-income working parents with employer-sponsored childcare rather than low-income families. No bill sponsorships or floor statements specifically addressing Head Start, universal pre-K, or childcare deserts have been identified in 2026. The federal FY2026 funding bill boosted investment in child care and early learning programs, but Hagerty was not among members who signed letters calling for increased funding.

child_hunger.summary: Hagerty voted for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (July 2025), which enacted the largest SNAP cuts in the program's history — approximately $187 billion over 10 years. As of May 2026, approximately 16% of Tennessee SNAP beneficiaries have already lost benefits, and Tennessee faces over $110 million in new annual costs shifted from the federal government. Advocacy groups protested outside his Nashville office, and national data confirm 3.5 million Americans have lost SNAP access since July 2025.
child_hunger.details: The OBBB, which Hagerty voted for on July 1, 2025 (Senate passed 51-50 with VP Vance casting the tiebreaker), cut SNAP by $187 billion over a decade — the biggest cut in the program's history per the CBO. New work requirements now extend to adults ages 55-64 and parents of children 14 and up. States with error rates above 6% must now cover up to 15% of benefit costs, putting Tennessee on the hook for an estimated $110 million+ annually. CNBC reported on May 30, 2026 that 3.5 million Americans nationally have lost SNAP access since July 2025, with Tennessee seeing roughly a 16% decline in SNAP enrollment. The Tennessee Commission on Children and Youth highlighted the fiscal burden. About 130,000 Tennessee households with children could lose some or all SNAP benefits, per CBPP. WBIR reached out to Hagerty for comment on the Tennessee fiscal impact but received no response.

parental_support.summary: The OBBB Hagerty voted for raised the Child Tax Credit to $2,200 per child (permanent, inflation-indexed), quadrupled the employer childcare credit, created a PFML credit, and established Trump Accounts. However, the CTC expansion does not increase benefits for the estimated 17 million children in families too poor to claim the full credit. His February 2026 floor remarks emphasized parental rights in education and school choice rather than economic supports for parents.
parental_support.details: The One Big Beautiful Bill Act included a CTC increase to $2,200 per child (permanent and inflation-indexed); analysis by the Tax Policy Center notes neither the House nor Senate plans increased refundability for the ~17 million lowest-income children who currently receive less than the $2,000 maximum credit. Hagerty's February 5, 2026 Senate floor statement focused on school choice and parental rights in education, noting Tennessee received 54,000 applications for 20,000 Education Freedom Scholarship spots. He framed the OBBB in a June 30, 2025 Bloomberg TV appearance primarily as a tax cut and anti-tax-increase measure, not explicitly addressing family economic supports. The quadrupled employer childcare credit and PFML credit in OBBB are supply-side mechanisms that primarily benefit employers and higher-income families with employer-sponsored benefits.

name: Marquita Bradshaw
bio: Memphis environmental justice activist who won the 2020 Democratic primary against expectations. Running again on environmental and economic-justice platform.
photo_credit: Bradshaw for Senate official campaign website

early_childhood_ed.summary: Bradshaw supports universal pre-K education and quality childcare as part of a broader platform calling for funding public education at levels comparable to military spending. These positions, first articulated during her 2020 campaign and reaffirmed on her current 2026 campaign website, represent her most recent public stance; no new 2025-2026 specific statements on early childhood education were found.
early_childhood_ed.details: Bradshaw's campaign website at marquitabradshaw.com consistently reflects support for universal pre-K, quality childcare, and high-quality public education from pre-K through grade 12. Her signature framing — 'I am a lifelong proponent of funding our education system the same as we do our military' — appears on her current issues page. Her 2020 platform explicitly listed 'Fund universal pre-K education' and 'Provide quality childcare.' As a single working-class mother who raised her son in Memphis, she has drawn personal connections between access to childcare and economic opportunity. No 2025-2026 press releases or campaign announcements specifically addressing Head Start funding levels or childcare cost legislation were found.

child_hunger.summary: No specific 2025-2026 public statements from Bradshaw on child hunger, SNAP, Summer EBT, or school nutrition programs were found. Her broader platform emphasizes working-class economic justice and healthcare access, but she has not issued candidate statements addressing Tennessee's Summer EBT opt-out controversy or the SNAP cuts enacted through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
child_hunger.details: Research through June 2026 found no press releases, social media posts, or campaign statements from Marquita Bradshaw specifically addressing SNAP, Summer EBT, child hunger, or school nutrition programs. This is notable given the significant Tennessee-specific child hunger debate: Governor Lee's decision to opt out of the $84 million federal Summer EBT program for a second consecutive summer (affecting roughly 700,000 children), the OBBB's $187 billion SNAP cut package, and bipartisan state-level pushback including the $7 million budget allocation for S-EBT in 2027. Bradshaw's OnTheIssues Families & Children page shows no stance on record.

parental_support.summary: Bradshaw supports a $15 minimum wage, healthcare for all, and high-quality public education as her core economic support mechanisms for working families. No specific positions on paid family leave, the Child Tax Credit, or direct childcare cost programs were found in 2025-2026 research.
parental_support.details: Bradshaw's current campaign issues page calls for 'fully and aggressively fighting for the federal recognition and implementation of a living wage beginning at immediately increasing the minimum wage to $15.00 an hour.' Her 2020 platform included 'relieve current student debt, provide quality childcare' as part of her economic agenda. No 2025-2026 press releases or campaign statements addressing the OBBB's child tax credit provisions, federal paid leave legislation, or childcare affordability were found. OnTheIssues records no stance from Bradshaw on the child tax credit, paid family leave, or childcare cost subsidy programs.

name: Maria Brewer
bio: Longtime Tennessee Democratic Party staffer making her first run for federal office.

early_childhood_ed.summary: Brewer's campaign website explicitly lists support for early childhood education and pre-K access as part of her education platform, making this a newly documented position. No details on funding levels, program specifics, or legislative proposals have been published.
early_childhood_ed.details: The issues page at mariabrewerforsenate.com states Brewer supports investing in 'early childhood education and pre-K access' as part of her education policy platform. This is the first confirmed specific policy position on early childhood education documented for her 2026 campaign. No additional detail on Head Start, childcare deserts, childcare workforce, or funding mechanisms appears on her site. Her April 25, 2026 Loyal Opposition podcast appearance focused on healthcare and cost of living without addressing early childhood specifically. She is a former Tennessee Democratic Party Director of Party Affairs running in the August 6, 2026 Democratic primary.

child_hunger.summary: No specific position on child hunger, SNAP, or food assistance was found on Brewer's campaign website or in any 2026 public statements. Her platform addresses grocery affordability broadly but does not mention SNAP cuts or Summer EBT.
child_hunger.details: Brewer's campaign site discusses cost-of-living concerns and grocery affordability as part of a broader economic platform but does not specifically address SNAP, Summer EBT, or child hunger programs. No press releases, media appearances, or social media posts from May-June 2026 on these topics were surfaced. Tennessee is experiencing significant child hunger disruption in 2026 — including no Summer EBT for the second consecutive summer and a 16% drop in SNAP enrollment — but Brewer has not been documented responding publicly to these developments. Her framing as 'daughter, mom, wife running for working families' suggests potential alignment with food security issues, but no stated positions exist.

parental_support.summary: Brewer's campaign website indicates she supports families with young children keeping more take-home pay rather than waiting for annual tax credits, suggesting implicit support for immediate income support over CTC-style annual refunds. No specific positions on paid family leave or childcare credits were found.
parental_support.details: The issues section of mariabrewerforsenate.com contains language that 'families with young children and low income need to keep their pay, not just get credits once a year,' which implies a preference for wage-based income supports (such as an expanded EITC or higher minimum wage) over annual refundable tax credits like the CTC. No specific positions on paid family medical leave, employer childcare credits, or childcare subsidy programs appear on her site. She identifies herself as a mom and frames her candidacy around working families but has not issued specific policy proposals on parental economic supports in the May-June 2026 period.

His FEC profile (candidate ID S6TN00323) confirms $0 in contributions for 2026. No Federalist Party national platform materials addressing child nutrition were located.
